extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, breeders, horticulturists, and educated readers interested in variation and selection
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and theoretical principles governing how selection (methodical and unconscious) and variability produce changed breeds, varieties, and species in plants and animals; aimed at guiding observation, breeding practice, and taxonomic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breeder qualifications (accuracy of eye and judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not one man in a thousand has accuracy of eye and judgment sufficient to become an eminent breeder. If gifted with these qualities, and he studies his subject for years, and devotes his lifetime to it with indomitable perseverance, he will succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful improvement by selection requires acute observation, sound judgment, long study, and persistent effort; skill is developed by years of practice (example: few become skilful pigeon-fanciers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodical versus unconscious selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection may be methodical (intentional, with a distinct object) or Unconscious (resulting from everyone trying to possess and breed from the best individuals without intending to alter the breed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both forms are important; unconscious selection, carried over long periods by many people, can produce substantial change (examples: Bakewell's and Collins' work vs. slow improvements like King Charles's spaniel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection acts only on pre-existing variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Man can never act by selection, excepting on variations which are first given to him in some slight degree by nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breeders cannot create novel characters by will; they can only amplify slight natural deviations (examples: the origin of fantails or pouter-pigeons from slight initial deviations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Large population size increases chance of useful variations
rubrics_metrics.description: The chance of their appearance will be much increased by a large number of individuals being kept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raising large stocks (e.g., by nurserymen) gives more opportunities for rare useful variations to appear; small lots (e.g., poor people’s flocks) hinder improvement (Marshall’s remark on Yorkshire sheep).

rubrics_metrics.name: Close attention to slight deviations is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: The animal or plant should be so highly useful to man, or so much valued by him, that the closest attention should be paid to even the slightest deviation in the qualities or structure of each individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without careful scrutiny and selection of small improvements no progress occurs (example: the strawberry varied but only improved markedly once gardeners attended to slight differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention of unwanted crosses (breeding control)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of animals with separate sexes, facility in preventing crosses is an important element of success in the formation of new races.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enclosure and mating systems matter: pigeons (mate for life) can have many true races in the same aviary; wandering or nocturnal species (cats) are hard to keep pure-bred; management influences ability to maintain breeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of propagation and ability to cull aids selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Pigeons can be propagated in great numbers and at a very quick rate, and inferior birds may be freely rejected, as when killed they serve for food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Species that breed fast and can have inferior individuals culled are easier to improve; by contrast, species that are hard to rear or kept in small numbers produce fewer distinct breeds (examples: peacocks, geese, donkeys, cats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of growth (correlated responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of correlation of growth ... will ensure some differences; continued selection of slight variations in one part will produce races differing chiefly in these characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting for one trait often produces changes in other traits; selection largely acts on externally visible characters because internal traits are harder to select for—expect correlated changes and unintended effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of accumulated change requires records
rubrics_metrics.description: Slow and insensible changes of this kind could never be recognised unless actual measurements or careful drawings of the breeds in question had been made long ago, which might serve for comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical records, measurements and drawings enable detection of gradual change over generations (examples: comparing florists' flowers or pigeons with old treatises).

rubrics_metrics.name: Small initial deviations can lead to major long-term change
rubrics_metrics.description: The man who first selected a pigeon with a slightly larger tail, never dreamed what the descendants of that pigeon would become through long-continued, partly unconscious and partly methodical selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even minute variations, if continually selected, can accumulate into extreme and novel forms over many generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of crossing depends on mode of propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: When in any country several domestic breeds have once been established, their occasional intercrossing, with the aid of selection, has, no doubt, largely aided in the formation of new sub-breeds; but the importance of the crossing of varieties has, I believe, been greatly exaggerated, both in regard to animals and to those plants which are propagated by seed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crossing is comparatively less important for seed-propagated plants but is of immense importance in plants propagated by cuttings, buds, etc., where hybrids and mongrels' variability and sterility are less troublesome to cultivators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability is influenced by conditions of life, inheritance, and reversion
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditions of life, from their action on the reproductive system, are so far of the highest importance as causing variability. ... The effects of variability are modified by various degrees of inheritance and of reversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand multiple causes of variability (environmental conditions, inheritance patterns, reversion) and that outcomes are complex and not solely due to one factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual differences supply raw material for selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual differences ... are highly important for us, as they afford materials for natural selection to accumulate, in the same manner as man can accumulate ... individual differences in his domesticated productions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even small, often overlooked differences among offspring are crucial for selection; systematists may ignore them, but they are the starting point for varieties and species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polymorphic genera complicate species-versus-variety judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Those genera which have sometimes been called 'protean' or 'polymorphic' ... in which the species present an inordinate amount of variation; and hardly two naturalists can agree which forms to rank as species and which as varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In genera like Rubus, Rosa, Hieracium, many intermediate and variable forms exist; such intrinsic polymorphism may be independent of conditions of life and not shaped by selection, complicating taxonomic ranks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomic ranks (species vs variety) are partly arbitrary and require expert consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: The term species ... is one arbitrarily given for the sake of convenience ... in determining whether a form should be ranked as a species or a variety, the opinion of naturalists having sound judgment and wide experience seems the only guide to follow. We must, however, in many cases, decide by a majority of naturalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use broad experience, analogy, and consensus rather than rigid definitions when deciding species versus variety; expect disagreement among competent naturalists and rely on accumulated knowledge and majority judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wide range and commonness correlate with greater variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Wide ranging, much diffused, and common species vary most. Species of the larger genera in any country vary more than the species of the smaller genera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying variation expect more diversity in widespread/common species and in species belonging to large genera; distribution and genus size are useful heuristics for anticipating variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Young observers tend to over-split species; broaden sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: When a young naturalist commences the study of a group of organisms quite unknown to him, he is at first much perplexed ... His general tendency will be to make many species ... As he extends the range of his observations, he will meet with more cases of difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid premature splitting: broaden geographic, taxonomic, and comparative sampling before erecting species; extend observations across regions and related groups to gain perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varieties can be incipient species but need not become species
rubrics_metrics.description: I look at varieties which are in any degree more distinct and permanent, as steps leading to more strongly marked and more permanent varieties; and at these latter, as leading to sub-species, and to species. It need not be supposed that all varieties or incipient species necessarily attain the rank of species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat well-marked varieties as potential early-stage species (incipient species), but recognize they may remain varieties, go extinct, or supplant parent species; classification should reflect possible dynamic outcomes.
